title: Regular Expressions
body:
The algebraic notation for [[Regular Languages]]. A [[DFA]] says how to *recognise* a
language; a regular expression says how to *build* it.

## The definition

Regular expressions over an [[Alphabet]] $\Sigma$ are defined inductively. Base cases:

- $\emptyset$, the empty language
- $\varepsilon$, the language $\{\varepsilon\}$
- $a$ for each $a \in \Sigma$, the language $\{a\}$

And three operations, in precedence order star > concatenation > union:

| Operation | Written | Language |
|---|---|---|
| union | $R_1 \cup R_2$, or $R_1 + R_2$, or a vertical bar in tools | $L(R_1) \cup L(R_2)$ |
| concatenation | $R_1 R_2$ | every $xy$ with $x \in L(R_1)$, $y \in L(R_2)$ |
| Kleene star | $R^*$ | zero or more copies of $R$ concatenated |

That is the whole language. Three operators, and the closure properties of the regular
languages are exactly why they are the three.

Note $R^*$ always includes $\varepsilon$, and $\emptyset^* = \{\varepsilon\}$. Both are
standard trick questions.

## Examples

```
(0|1)*              every binary string
(0|1)*11            binary strings ending in 11
0*10*10*            exactly two 1s
(aa)*               even-length strings of a
a(a|b)*b            starts with a, ends with b
```

## Kleene's theorem

> A language is describable by a regular expression if and only if it is recognised by a
> finite automaton.

Both directions are constructions you should be able to run:

- **Regex → [[NFA]]** (Thompson's construction): one small gadget per operator, wired together
  with $\varepsilon$-transitions. Recursion over the inductive definition above, so it falls
  out of the syntax.
- **[[DFA]] → regex** (state elimination): rip out states one at a time, relabelling the
  remaining arrows with regular expressions until only start and accept are left.

Combined with the subset construction from [[NFA]], all three notations collapse into one
class. That is the central result of the first half of [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]].

## Theory vs. the ones you actually type

The regexes in `grep`, JavaScript, and every text editor add backreferences (`\1`),
lookahead, and lazy quantifiers. Backreferences in particular are **not** regular: `(a*)b\1`
matches $\{a^n b a^n\}$, which the [[Pumping Lemma]] kills. So "regex" in practice describes a
strictly larger and much slower class than the object in this course, and the ones that stay
within theory can be matched in linear time by conversion to a DFA. Everything above is the
theoretical version.

## Core Facts to Know

- Base cases are $\emptyset$, $\varepsilon$, and single symbols.
- Operations are union, concatenation, and Kleene star. Nothing else.
- Precedence: star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union.
- $R^*$ includes the empty string; $\emptyset^* = \{\varepsilon\}$.
- **Kleene's theorem**: regular expressions and finite automata describe the same languages.
- Regex → NFA is Thompson's construction, using $\varepsilon$-transitions.
- DFA → regex is state elimination.
- Backreferences make practical regexes non-regular.
